summary: Retires the MD2 message digest algorithm and discusses why, moving RFC 1319 to Historic status. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: MD2 turns a message into a 128-bit digest, but researchers found weaknesses in the algorithm. RFC 6149 moves its original specification to Historic status and says not to use MD2 for digital signatures.

questions: why was md2 moved to historic status
is md2 safe for digital signatures
subtitle: Why the MD2 message-digest algorithm and its original RFC were retired.

tldr.problem: MD2 has weaknesses in its collision and pre-image resistance, and older RFCs still referred to it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6149 reviews the attacks and the impact on documents that mention MD2, then moves RFC 1319 to Historic status.
tldr.outcome: The RFC says MD2 must not be used for digital signatures and recommends replacing it with an existing hash such as SHA-256.

today: RFC 6149 moves RFC 1319 to Historic status. RFC 6149 is Informational and recommends replacing MD2 with an existing hash algorithm such as SHA-256.

sections.title: Retiring the MD2 Digest
sections.content:
MD2 takes a message of any length and produces a 128-bit message digest. RFC 6149 retires MD2 by moving RFC 1319 to Historic status and explains the reasons for that decision.

The RFC reviews the documents that still specified MD2 and describes the effect of retiring it. It notes that some references retained MD2 for compatibility, while others had already dropped it or preferred another algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: MD2 produces a short digest from a message. This RFC explains why the original MD2 specification should no longer be treated as current.

sections.title: Why MD2 Is No Longer Recommended
sections.content:
Studies cited by the RFC found that MD2 is not collision-free and that pre-image and second pre-image attacks are possible. A collision is two different messages with the same digest; a pre-image attack works backward from a digest to a message.

The RFC also says MD2 is slower than MD4 and MD5 on the machines those algorithms target, and slower than the listed Secure Hash Standard algorithms. It recommends moving away from MD2 before a severe break makes withdrawal urgent.
sections.plainLanguage: MD2 does not provide the hash properties that applications need for important security uses. The RFC recommends replacing it rather than waiting for a more serious failure.

sections.title: Effect on Documents That Mention MD2
sections.content:
The RFC lists Proposed Standard, Informational, and Experimental RFCs that specified MD2. It describes the impact of changing MD2's status as minimal: in some protocols support had already been dropped, while other documents retained it only for compatibility or made another algorithm preferred.

The RFC says the Secure HyperText Transfer Protocol document was largely supplanted by HTTP over TLS. It also notes that the cited documents had varying reasons for keeping or dropping MD2 support.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC checks which earlier documents mention MD2 and explains what retiring it means for them. Several had already reduced or ended their reliance on MD2.

sections.title: Attack Results and the Recommendation
sections.content:
The RFC reports that an attack without MD2's nonlinear checksum can find a collision in 2^12 MD2 operations. With the checksum, the best collision attack it cites takes 2^63.3 operations and 2^50 memory. It identifies the stronger concern as MD2 not being one-way: the cited improved pre-image attack takes 2^73 operations.

A pre-image attack can also find a second pre-image, which the RFC says is more serious for digital signatures than a collision attack. Therefore MD2 must not be used for digital signatures. The document recommends deprecating MD2 in favor of existing hash algorithms such as SHA-256.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC's main concern is that attackers can work backward from an MD2 digest more easily than a secure hash should allow. It says not to use MD2 for digital signatures and recommends moving to another hash.

references.text: Kaliski, B., "The MD2 Message-Digest Algorithm", RFC 1319, April 1992.
